en: The Treasure Store Treatise, composed by the Śramaṇa Shi Sengzhao of Chang’an.
Chapter One: Illuminating the Extent of Emptiness and Existence.
That which is empty is emptiness, yet it is not true emptiness;
that which is form is form, yet it is not true form.
True form is formless.
True emptiness has no name;
it is the father of names.
It has no form; it is the mother of forms.
He is the source and root of all things,
the primordial ancestor of Heaven and Earth;
above, he bestows the profound celestial phenomena.
Descending below, one reaches the Hall of Darkness.
Primordial Qi is contained within the Great Image;
the Great Image is hidden within the Formless.
To recognize the spirit of things:
within the spirit there is a deity;
within the deity there is a body.
Unconditioned and transformative,
each accords with spontaneity;
though there are subtle functions and applications.
Gradually there arose forms and names;
yet while form had not yet emerged from its essence,
name had not yet arisen from what is nameless.
The manifestations of forms have already appeared;
wandering vapors disturb the clarity.
It is silent and vast.
Vast and expansive!
Divided and distinct!
Above, there is a ruler.
Below, there are ministers;
fathers and sons share intimacy in their dwellings,
while those of high and low status differ in their positions.
The establishment of the teaching describes its causes;
thereafter, the state demarcates its borders and the people organize themselves into households.
Each maintained their respective positions;
rites and righteousness flourished and were practiced;
there were virtuous deeds worthy of praise.
There is evil that can be named;
it is esteemed by the virtuous and despised by the wicked.
Thereupon, what is non-existent immediately gives rise to contention;
the wise possess liberation,
while the foolish are bound.
Above, one assumes a burdensome form;
below, there is no tranquil joy.
One loses the aspiration for spontaneity.
They violate the covenant beyond the phenomenal world;
they are deluded regarding the action of non-action,
and they engage in the activity of conditioned creation.
Once his teachings and instructions had been put into practice,
he caused those above and below to respond in harmony; thus, the five musical notes were established as sounds,
and the five colors were established as forms.
The five behaviors are established as the five conducts;
the five virtues are established as the five virtues.
To differ by even a hair's breadth [is a grave error].
Transgressions are as vast as mountains;
the Vinaya prohibits them before they occur,
so as to prevent what one has not yet desired to do.
There is no breadth that allows for license;
there is a constraint imposed by manifold circumstances.
The reason for this is as follows:
When people do not know contentment,
this constitutes a time of turbidity and disorder.
To have a younger brother and a teacher— this is the way.
The teacher has that upon which to instruct;
the disciple has that upon which to rely.
Heaven and earth are vast and desolate.
The universe is vast and expansive;
within it there is smoke and dust,
and the pure void is obscured by a film.
Its majestic form possesses inner divinity and outer numinosity;
yet one falsely entertains thoughts and deliberations.
The true is utterly obscure;
its false consciousness exists,
and its true nature is deluded.
It is not grasped yet is grasped;
it is not attained yet is attained.
Therefore, the principle is inexhaustible.
Things are thus without limit;
they move and are chaotic,
internally giving rise to the three poisons.
Beholding and listening—
externally receiving the five desires,
the mind becomes frantic and unsettled.
His body is restless;
whatever it touches, it moves,
like a blazing fire.
Therefore, the Sage established the orthodox teaching and set forth the true plan,
so that those companions who lack knowledge [may be guided].
Above and below depend on one another;
cultivate non-action and bring rest to all that remains.
Gradually one arrives at suchness;
the principle of suchness is identical to the fundamental, true path.
It cannot be realized through cultivation,
nor can it be sought through aspiration;
it is solely the nature of quiescent extinction.
Now, that which is "Real" has no continent and no island;
it has no companion and no associate.
Boundless and limitless,
without location or abode,
it is able to serve as the progenitor of all things.
It is not seen by the eye;
it is not heard by the ear;
it is not form or color.
It is not a phantom soul;
it can serve as the root-gate of the triple world.
That which is correct first leaves the physical form.
Next, extinguish all sentiments;
do not rely on external objects,
and do not be constrained by the cycle of birth.
It can harmonize with the Great Way and communicate with the spiritual intelligences.
That which has function is called "spirit" (shen);
that which has form is called "body" (shen).
That which is unconditioned is called the Way;
that which is signless is called the Real.
These are names applied in response to phenomena.
It is fashioned according to things;
it is eternally abiding and eternally present,
neither born nor aging.
In principle, it accords with ten thousand virtues;
in practice, it issues from a thousand ingenuities. Though such matters are inexhaustible, [the essence remains constant].
The principle ultimately constitutes a single path;
there is no one who realizes it,
and there is no one who attains it.
Yet, they do not realize or attain [this],
remaining constantly in mental delusion;
their minds are not true.
They delude and confuse other people;
they are dazed and bewildered,
as if possessed by malevolent spirits.
It appears as though there is thought;
yet when one investigates and analyzes it,
there is nothing at all to point out or take hold of.
Like clouds suddenly appearing in the sky,
like dust suddenly settling on a mirror;
both arise through mutual conditionality.
Yet they falsely maintain this existence.
To have delusion is called ignorance;
to be without delusion is called truth.
True ice is released water;
delusive water freezes into ice.
These two—ice and water—are one.
Their essence is not different.
Delusion regarding it is called ignorance;
awakening to its reality is called wisdom.
Its ice cannot be melted in winter;
its water cannot be frozen in spring.
Thus, a fool cannot be reformed immediately.
Wisdom cannot be attained instantaneously;
it is gradually explained and gradually dissolved until it merges with the great ocean.
This may be called the Way of spontaneity;
its operation is profound and mysterious,
beyond the reach of thought and deliberation.
One should practice with continuity,
not with frantic exertion;
for such is the way to advance upon the Path.
Among these are ten thousand paths:
the exhausted fish rests in a drop of water;
the sick bird perches upon a reed.
These two do not recognize the great ocean,
nor do they recognize the vast forest;
that the person pursues a minor path is likewise the case with their underlying principle.
This may be called halting mid-course after long effort;
failing to reach accord with reality,
one abandons the great for the sake of the small.
To rely on support halfway along the path is to find peace through minor peace;
it does not equal finding peace through great peace.
In its greatness, it is vast and boundless;
all sentient beings are of one body,
and all things share the same heart.
In responding, there are a thousand transformations;
in manifesting, there are myriad appearances.
Yet it neither emerges nor perishes.
Its application is uninterrupted;
it possesses mind but lacks form.
It has function but no person.
Manifesting birth while being unborn;
manifesting a body while being bodiless;
eternally fathoming the unfathomable.
Ordinary knowledge is not recognized;
there is action, yet no action;
there is attainment, yet no attainment.
The reflections in a mirror manifest in a thousand ways;
the nature of water displays ten thousand colors;
and shadows divide the realm of dust.
Its application is infinite.
It is formless yet takes form;
it is nameless yet receives names.
Things of similar categories resonate with one another;
through their harmonious union they arise,
yet though they arise, they do not truly arise.
He is without a sentient being;
the multitude calls him a sage,
and the multitude calls him enlightened.
Although there are various titles,
each according to its name,
this is their reality.
Taking non-action as its fundamental principle and formlessness as its manifestation,
it is equal to pure vacuity.
It is identical to the great void;
when investigated, it has no location,
yet its function operates within it.
That which is attained is one;
that which is realized is subtle.
As for attainment, it is not uniform.
If one realizes it, it is not secret;
yet it is not not one.
Yet it is not not secret.
Its substance is yin and detached;
its function is yang and subtle.
Words cannot fully exhaust its principle.
To exhaustively perform every ritual protocol would be called "excessive refinement. Indeed,
the herbs upon the mountains are infinite.
The spring water never runs dry;
the valley breeze never ceases;
the sound of the bells never stops.
If even material things are like this,
how much more so the Way?
That which exists must inevitably perish quickly.
Nothing is necessarily eternal.
Though heaven and earth undergo change,
empty space alone remains constant.
Now, those who study the Way practice until there is nothing remaining;
those who do not study the Way practice with something remaining.
The Way without remainder is near.
There are other paths that are coarse:
they know existence as subject to destruction,
and they know non-existence as subject to decay.
The knowledge of true gnosis does not calculate existence or non-existence;
it regards existence as non-existence.
In non-existence there is no non-existence;
existence and non-existence are not perceived.
Nature and characteristics are suchness.
It is silent and devoid of things,
yet it functions and emerges; were it not so, [it could not do so].
There is much delusion and much loss;
within this there are dreams and anxieties,
which primarily give rise to various ailments.
What is not ominous is treated as ominous;
what is not auspicious is treated as auspicious.
Such are the matters of fortune and misfortune.
Obscuring the true oneness,
those who practice the Way must not share in such delusion.
Now, there are three types of those who study the Way.
The first is called the True;
the second is called the Adjacent.
The third is called "hearing.
To study and practice is called "hearing";
to sever all study is called "the neighbor."
That which transcends these two is called the True.
There are likewise three types of those who do not study the Way;
the highest among them is called the Auspicious.
The next grade is called "good";
the lowest grade is called "calamity.
Ultimate bliss is called "good."
Extreme suffering is called calamity;
neither-suffering-nor-pleasure is called auspiciousness.
Yet these three do not enter into the Truth.
To constantly act thus is to be contrary to the Way.
When the spirit soars into the vast expanse,
the winds and waves of the sea surge in turmoil.
The mind and its objects are agitated and disturbed.
How tragic, how lamentable!
This is the cycle of rebirth within the three realms.
Appearing and disappearing within birth and death,
coming and going through the six realms,
they cannot be saved by the Way.
One cannot depart with the Truth;
riding upon the Holy One, we share in universal compassion,
like a mother mindful of her infant.
Therefore, the cessation of transformation was not for its own time;
he waited with patience until the opportune moment arrived.
Such is the nature of the Great Way.
The ritual protocols of antiquity and the present are identical;
one must not act with casual haste,
nor may one proceed with reckless impetuosity.
Within divinity there is wisdom;
within wisdom there is compassion;
yet compassion cannot save them.
One merely exhausts oneself in vain. Yet,
believing that one can attain liberation,
one continues to practice as before.
Scrutinizing with diligent effort,
one constantly gives rise to anxious thoughts;
filled with dread, one searches outwardly.
They have strayed from the profound path;
turbidity and defilement have sullied the pure void;
their minds remain attached to worldly existence.
Alas, how bitter! One cannot escape the burden of worldly affairs;
indeed, the sun is hidden within the clouds.
Though luminous, it does not illuminate;
the treasury of wisdom remains within delusion.
Though true, it does not manifest as the Way.
Why is this so? Because they have not yet emerged from the entanglements.
Therefore, being distant, they cannot be reconciled.
One must not abandon one's parents;
as for those who have not yet attained the Way,
one must not act recklessly toward them.
Now, one who has resolved to retreat pays no heed to what lies behind;
one who has resolved for battle pays no heed to his own head.
One who resolves matters of learning does not value them for the sake of the self;
one who resolves the Way does not value it for the sake of affairs.
Their entry leaves no trace.
When it emerges, there is nothing to be sought;
it is utterly ungraspable. As攀緣 (pān-yuán, object-dependent clinging) naturally subsides, it is quiescent.
Quiescent and non-arising,
its own essence is nameless;
it is the uncarved block of namelessness.
In principle, there are no external desires;
the merits as numerous as the sands of the Ganges are perfectly and naturally complete.
Now, those who dwell within a shell do not know the vastness of the universe; those whose forms are confined [to a body] likewise [do not know it].
Because one does not know the vastness of space,
there is no darkness within light,
and no light within darkness.
All dharmas arise and perish from moment to moment,
each without waiting for the other;
things are separated and the mind is detached.
This contradicts common sense and is difficult to reconcile.
Now, a red jujube containing a worm has its interior decayed while its exterior remains swollen.
Sand and water flow together;
the upper part is clear while the lower is thick.
A state stores [treasures] with the sycophantic.
The world is not governed by the Way;
its form is hidden within the mind,
and all things become licentious.
The reason for this is that because there is illness,
things possess spiritual efficacy.
Spiritual beings must have demons;
demons must have desires;
desires must have minds.
The mind must possess emotion;
when emotion moves, it becomes desire;
when its aberrations manifest, they become vital essence (*jing*).
The essence is deluded by the spirit;
desire is deluded by the truth.
Therefore, for one who practices the Way:
It cannot be compared to a neighbor.
Now, when an ancient mirror reflects a spirit,
that spirit manifests its own form.
The ancient teachings illuminate the mind,
and that mind becomes naturally clear. Now,
taking heaven and earth as the upper and lower limits, [the cosmos is established].
In relation to the sun and moon, there are east and west;
in relation to the body, there are this and that;
in relation to the mind, there are right and wrong.
If there is neither "this" nor "that," what purpose do "is" and "is not" serve?
It is simply that things change according to the fluctuations of the mind.
Emotions shift as they pursue external objects;
both internal and external states are set in motion.
Consciousness rides upon these objects, galloping along.
In life one is a human;
in death one is a soul (ātmā).
These states are similar and continue in succession.
The dream possesses a physical body;
in reality, that is not this, and this is not that.
The bird-tracks and empty patterns manifest as something marvelous;
they are inconceivable and beyond discussion.
The Yin receives the retribution for the Yang’s bestowal;
though the path of the unseen is formless and elusive,
cause and effect bind one of their own accord.
These matters are like illusions;
they are variously modeled after reflections,
mirages, water, and the city of the Gandharvas.
Since none of these are realized,
they are called unreal;
they merely delude other people.
The principle of pure emptiness is ultimately bodiless.
As for supernatural powers and transformations—
It is like a dragon ascending to heaven;
it is like clouds gathering to cover the universe—
these are not yet worthy of esteem.
This cannot yet be considered true.
If one takes this as reality,
it is not yet the Way.
Some possess forms that are beautiful;
some possess speech that is eloquent;
some possess intelligence that is keen.
Some may be useful and skillful;
yet, if one takes them as the Way,
it is still not considered good.
That which exists is necessarily not true;
that which is created is necessarily not eternal.
Even heaven and earth shall eventually perish.
How rigid are material objects!
Only the Way has no root;
it is empty and profound, eternally abiding.
Only the Way has no substance;
it is subtle, wondrous, eternal, and true.
Only the Way has no affairs.
Throughout antiquity and the present, it has always been held in high esteem: only the Way is mindless,
yet all things are perfectly complete within it.
Therefore, the Way is without marks and without form;
it is without activity, without intention, and without mind,
yet it skillfully benefits all classes of beings.
He leads and benefits human relations;
it may be said that there are no creatures that do not submit to him.
Indeed, all things have their companions.
Only the Way alone remains;
beyond it there is nothing else,
and within it there is nothing further.
Without interior or exterior,
it encompasses the Grand Unity and pervades the eight mysteries.
It encompasses all things;
its form is neither internal nor external,
neither small nor large.
It is neither one nor different;
neither luminous nor obscure; neither arising nor ceasing;
neither coarse nor subtle.
Neither empty nor existent;
neither opening nor closing;
neither above nor below.
Neither formed nor destroyed;
neither moving nor still;
neither returning nor departing.
Neither deep nor shallow;
neither ignorant nor wise;
neither contrary nor compliant.
Neither permeable nor obstructed;
neither poor nor wealthy;
neither new nor old.
Neither good nor bad;
neither hard nor soft;
neither solitary nor paired.
The reason for this is that,
if one speaks of its interior,
it universally encompasses the Dharma-realm.
If one says it is external,
it fully corresponds to and carries the physical form;
if one says it is small...
It wraps everything ever more extensively;
yet if one speaks of its vastness,
it again enters the realm of atoms.
If one says they are identical,
each would simply follow its own nature;
if one says they are distinct...
The wondrous essence is devoid of substance;
if one speaks of its luminosity,
it is profound and darkly obscure.
If one says it is obscure,
it is brilliantly illuminated and penetratingly clear;
if one says it is born, [it is not so].
It is without state and without form;
yet if one speaks of its extinction,
it is eternally numinous throughout past and present.
If one says it is coarse,
it is subsumed within the realm of dust;
if one says it is subtle...
Though his body is as vast as a mountain,
if one speaks of its emptiness,
the myriad functions are contained within it.
If one says it exists, it is utterly silent and admits of no opening;
if one says it opens, [it is already closed].
It does not enter into the dust of the mundane world;
yet if one speaks of its closure,
its meaning extends beyond all limits.
If one says it is superior,
it is equal and signless;
if one says it is inferior...
Nothing can serve as a comparison for it.
If one were to speak of its formation,
it would be like striking down and scattering the myriad stars.
If one says it is destroyed,
it has remained constant since antiquity;
if one says it moves, [it remains unmoved].
Profoundly serene and grave;
yet if one were to say it is still,
all things are stirred in a state of bustling activity.
If one says they have returned,
they have gone without taking leave;
if one says they have departed, [they have not yet left].
Responding to things, he returns;
if one speaks of his profundity,
the myriad things share in his effortless functioning.
If one says they are shallow,
their roots cannot be traced;
if one says they are foolish, [they are not].
The methods of calculation number in the tens of thousands;
yet if one speaks of its wisdom,
it is tranquil and void, leaving nothing behind.
If one says it is contrary,
there is faith and reliance; if one says it is conformable, [there is likewise faith and reliance].
Nothing can restrain it;
yet if one speaks of its pervasiveness,
its subtle traces remain unfathomable.
If one says it is obstructed,
there is empty space for inhalation and exhalation;
if one says it is impoverished...
With ten thousand virtues and a thousand treasures,
if one were to speak of its wealth,
it would be so vast and peerless that no one could equal it.
If one says it is new,
it has ancient causes from the past;
if one says it is old, [it is nevertheless manifest now].
Nothing can defile it.
If one speaks of its excellence,
there is nothing by which it can be preserved.
If one says it is brittle,
its substance remains as it was at the beginning;
if one says it is hard, [it is so].
Though crushed, it is not harmed;
though called soft,
its strength is not diminished when bent.
If one says it is solitary,
there are beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges;
if one says it is paired, [it is not].
The True One is a solitary wheel;
thus, the Way cannot be expressed by a single name,
and its principle cannot be proclaimed through a single meaning.
I have merely set forth these teachings in brief;
how could I possibly exhaust their limits?
Therefore, [the heretics] resort to such acts as decapitation and reducing the body to ashes.
There is nothing that can diminish life;
there is nothing that the Golden Elixir and Jade Liquor do not provide for the nourishment of life.
Therefore, that which is truly born does not perish;
that which is truly extinguished is not born.
This may be called "eternal extinction."
This may be called "constant arising.
As for those who desire birth and seek the cessation of evil,
they do not realize that there is constant cessation.
Regarding the cessation of craving and the arising of non-evil: this is not awakening to the constant arising [of phenomena].
These two names, "delusion" and "awakening," [are merely conventional designations].
Failing to see true accomplishment,
the intent of grasping and rejecting follows deluded sentiments.
Therefore, that which is eternally empty does not exist,
and that which eternally exists is not empty;
these two do not depend upon one another.
Every sentence is the core essence.
Therefore, the sage follows the existence of the Way and its manifestations.
Following the path of emptiness, one realizes emptiness;
yet emptiness does not contradict existence,
nor does existence contradict emptiness.
Both expressions are free from fault,
and both meanings apply equally;
this extends even to the teaching of a self.
Nor does it contradict selflessness;
even when speaking of phenomena,
it does not contradict the absence of phenomena.
For this reason, one is not turned by words.
It is like casting gold into the form of a person;
one observes only the person.
One does not see its gold;
its name is delusive and its appearance is confusing.
The reason for this is that all have lost the truth;
thus, everything is an illusion.
All is false and unreal;
know that illusion is illusion.
Guard the truth and embrace the One.
Unstained by external things,
pure and void as the Grand One (Taiyi),
how could there be any loss?
The mind perishes and intention is lost;
the body is freed from all ailments,
and the single mark does not arise.
Whether it be tranquility or calamity,
if even good fortune does not follow,
what can be done about misfortune?
Regarding matters of fortune and misfortune,
both are without reliance.
Now, as for the path of entering the Way:
Internally empty and externally pure,
like water that has congealed into clarity,
the myriad phenomena are reflected in its radiance.
His intention is neither sunken nor is his mind floating;
it neither emerges nor enters.
Profoundly still and self-abiding,
neither internal nor external factors disturb it;
consciousness does not engage with objects.
Since each performs its own function,
what further need is there for words?
Indeed, fire does not depend on the sun to be hot.
The wind is cool without waiting for the moon;
a solid stone remains within the water;
though Heaven be blind, light still shines.
Light and darkness have always been thus;
dryness and moisture occupy the same space.
Even material things do not borrow from one another.
How much more so the Way!
The King regards all existence as his people,
and these people turn toward the King.
The King relies upon the people;
when they are united as one,
he is called the Buddha.
Solely honored throughout the three realms,
awakened to the non-existence of all things;
acting without acting.
Having completed all that was to be done,
the Teacher of Gods and Humans, the Perfectly Enlightened One, fully understood that his manifestations of provisional forms were now finished.
He guides all beings swiftly;
his principle is tranquil and void,
his radiance surpassing the sun of wisdom.
Universally illuminating the ten directions;
above harmonizing with the superior and below attaining auspiciousness; desiring nothing that differs from others.
One does not desire a different object;
one does not desire a different meaning;
one does not desire a different cause.
Equal and non-dual,
with a perfectly integrated single body—
this may be called the true nature of the Great Elephant.
This principle is difficult to perceive;
therefore, one employs provisional skillful means,
engaging in frequent interrogation and discourse.
It manifests according to things.
Now, that which one desires externally is the dust of the world;
that which one desires internally is the body.
The mind that desires is the desire realm;
that which grasps sensory objects is the form realm;
and that which relies on a physical body is the formless realm.
That which relies on the conceptualizing mind constitutes the formless realm;
the cessation of these three is called the Truth of the Path.
The truth of cessation is the Path.
However, this Path is provisional and not yet ultimate.
Empty and illusory;
the three realms are unreal.
Like a phantom and like a dream.
The six realms are devoid of substantiality;
not a single dharma is sent away,
nor is a single dharma attained.
One does not cultivate a single dharma,
nor does one realize a single dharma;
its nature is pure and naturally authentic.
Yet they claim to speak of the Great Way.
Therefore, if one surveys the world at large,
there are none who are not true men.
Who can grasp this principle and become one with that single category?
Those who study it are rare.
Those who attain it do so subtly;
it may be called vast and remote, difficult to know.
Those who know it take it as their teacher.
That which transforms is simple and plain;
it is without intentional action.
Though acting, it does nothing.
Acting without acting;
there is nothing that is not done. Harmonizing one's light and yielding to things as they are.
Things have no bonds.
Within the realm of heaven and earth,
amidst the expanse of the universe—
Within it lies a single treasure,
hidden within the mountain of form;
it is the numinous illumination that recognizes all things.
Both internally and externally it is empty;
it is still and silent, difficult to perceive.
Its name is the Mysterious and the Mysterious.
Skillfully emerging beyond the Purple Microcosm,
its function lies within the realm of the void;
it brings about transformation with absolute stillness.
Solitary and peerless,
his voice issues forth wondrous resonance,
and his countenance emits a radiant splendor.
Exhaustively observed, there is nothing to be seen;
it is given the provisional name "emptiness of emptiness," leaving behind only its sound.
One does not see their form;
only their achievement remains.
One does not see their countenance.
The hidden and the manifest are illuminated with clarity;
the principles of phenomena are empty and pervasive;
the myriad forms are sealed by the precious seal.
The true principle of the myriad phenomena:
when active, it takes form;
when quiescent, it is profound stillness.
Inherently pure yet not polished by artifice,
it is spontaneously perfected by the nature of reality;
its radiance transcends that of the sun and moon.
Virtue transcends the Great Clarity;
the myriad things are without activity,
and all are without name.
Transforming heaven and earth,
acting with sovereign ease in every direction;
the wondrous functions are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
It was formed from primordial chaos.
Who would not rejoice upon hearing this?
Who would not be struck with wonder upon hearing this?
How is it that this priceless treasure remains hidden within the pit of the aggregates and sense-bases? Alas, alas!
To thus disparage oneself—
how tragic, how tragic!
How can darkness be made bright?
That jewel was brilliantly radiant and resplendent,
shining clearly throughout the ten directions;
it was profoundly still and motionless.
Its application is majestic and grand;
it responds to sounds and forms,
and it accords with both the Yin and the Yang.
It is extraordinary and rootless;
empty yet profoundly still, it exists eternally.
One cannot see it even by blinking one's eyes.
Even with ears pricked, one does not hear it.
Its origin is dark and obscure;
its transformation takes form.
In its manifestation it is sagely;
in its application it is numinous.
It may truly be called the essence of the Great Way.
Its essence is profoundly true;
it is the cause of all things,
remaining eternally and immutably present.
It shares the same category as the Way.
Therefore, a sutra says:
"In accordance with the purity of one's mind..."
Thus, the Buddha-field is pure;
all that is encompassed therein is employed,
and its name is "The Holy."
2. Chapter on the Purity of the Essence of Detachment and Subtlety. Second. Its entry is detachment;
its emergence is subtlety.
One knows that detachment lies beyond entry.
Dust has no basis; know that it emerges from within the subtle.
The mind has no purposeful action.
The inner mind has nothing to do;
various views cannot shift it.
External objects have nothing to rely upon.
The myriad phenomena cannot bind him;
the myriad phenomena cannot bind him.
His thoughts and deliberations do not gallop away.

Even the various śrāvakas who have realized the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) still possess a remainder;
this remains true even up to the bodhisattvas of the tenth stage.
All possess the subtle hindrance of the ground-abiding ignorance (*mūla-vyavasthita-avidyā*).
Therefore, one is taken as the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), two as the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*),
and three as the triple world (*traidhātuka*).
Regarding the term "unconditioned" (asaṃskṛta), there are two kinds:
first, the unconditioned of realized cessation (nirodha);
second, the unconditioned of original nature (prakṛti).
Regarding what is called "realizing the unconditioned cessation" (*asaṃskṛta-nirodha*):
it refers to the suchness (*tathatā*) of the essence of all noble ones (*ārya*) who have severed hindrances through the cultivation of the path.
Therefore, the Sūtra says: "All worthy ones and sages rely upon the unconditioned dharma."
Yet there is a nature of differentiation.
That which is fundamentally unconditioned is what is called the primordial *dharmatā*:
neither cultivated nor realized, it is not something joined by persons, nor is it something attained through phenomena.
The dharmas of persons are fundamentally empty; their essence is pure, the ultimate truth.
Thus, a sutra says: "The principle of the true mark is neither conditioned nor unconditioned;
it is neither this shore nor the other shore."
It does not abide in the middle stream;
therefore, because it is not conditioned (*saṃskṛta*),
it cannot be cultivated or studied.
Because it is not unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), it cannot be realized through cessation.
If there were cultivation and realization,
then its nature would not be fundamentally unconditioned.
Therefore, the Sūtra says: "All dharmas take non-arising as their fundamental principle.
If the principle itself does not arise, then there is no such thing as "non-arising.
Since neither arising nor non-arising can be established, they cannot serve as proof.
Why is this? If there is realization, there is birth; if there is no realization, there is no birth.
This is based upon the primordial profound darkness.
That which is non-arising is the primordial limit (*koṭi*).
It neither emerges nor perishes, being like empty space and beyond all comparison.
Yet all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) are false and unreal.
Existence and non-existence arise through dependence upon the provisional and the conditional.
When one exhaustively investigates their fundamental source and destination, they return to the original reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*).
It is only that all sentient beings have lost this original ground.
Seeking externally involves meandering hardships and arduous cultivation;
yet through many kalpas, one fails to awaken to the Truth.
Therefore, by seeking the branches with the root as the goal, these peripheral delusions are not the Reality.
Seeking the root through its branches, one finds that the root is empty and not substantial.
Now, as for this "root," it is precisely that which should not be sought. Why is this so?
The fundamental does not seek the fundamental;
it is like gold not seeking gold.
The derivative does not conform to cultivation.
Why is this? Because one does not seek the false through the false.
It is, for example, like a lump of clay, which cannot be turned into gold.
The phenomena of body and mind are illusory and unreal.
For the common person to cultivate the body and mind in search of the Way is like seeking gold within a lump of clay.
If body and mind were themselves the Way,
why would the Sages speak of transcending body and mind?
Therefore, we know they are not the Way.
If it is fundamentally true, there is likewise no need for cultivation.
Why? Because there is no duality of dharmas.
Now, the Sage is not existent when born and not non-existent when dead.
He is devoid of the deluded mind of grasping and rejecting.
This so-called cycle of myriad births and deaths is fundamentally impartial and without partiality.
In the natural state of dharmatā, there is no self that acts;
it is only because those deluded beings give rise to false imaginings within themselves that various deluded minds and views arise.
Therefore, these are not real and they cannot be clearly understood.
Yet its fundamental limit is intrinsically pure;
subtle, profound, and in essence free from defilement.
Therefore, the various discourses of the thousands of sages and myriad worthies [concern it].
All these are expedient teachings regarding the real as non-real, and teachings regarding the non-transformed as transformed.
Therefore, where the ultimate limit is nameless, one names that which is nameless;
where the ultimate limit is signless, one names that which is signless.
Once names and forms are established, delusive confusion arises;
the principle of true oneness sinks, and the essence of the Way becomes obscured.
Therefore, the unnamable simplicity pervades all things and cannot be designated by any name.
Transcending the boundaries of measure, they are of one essence and non-dual.
Thus, a sutra says: "The myriad phenomena and the ten thousand images are all sealed by the One Dharma.
This "seal" is the primordial limit (*mūlakoṭi*).
However, the principle of the primordial limit (benji) is without self and without other, neither one nor different;
it encompasses the single vital breath (yiqi) and pervades all phenomena.
Furthermore, if there is a person whose intrinsic nature is pure,
who is born containing [this purity] and free from deluded thoughts within,
that person is a sage.
Yet, within the ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), there are no dharmas of a noble one (*ārya*) that differ by even so much as a mote of dust.
Furthermore, if there is a person whose intrinsic nature is pure, [they are likewise without such distinctions].
When one is born containing [the seeds of] delusion, the intermediate state of conceptualization arises;
with a self-nature thus turbid and confused, one becomes an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*).
Yet, within ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), there is no such thing as the dharma of an ordinary person.
There is not even as much difference as a single mote of dust.
Therefore, a sutra says: "The Buddha-nature is equal, vast, and immeasurable;
ordinary beings and sages are non-dual, and all are perfectly complete."
All grasses and trees are fully present, as are ants everywhere;
even down to the finest specks of dust and a single hair, there is nothing that does not contain the One within it.
Thus, a sutra says: "To thoroughly understand the One, all ten thousand things are exhausted."
Therefore, all sentient beings are born from the One Vehicle;
hence it is called the One Vehicle.
If one is deluded, there is differentiation; if one awakens, there is oneness.
The Sūtra says that the preceding thought is ordinary and the succeeding thought is holy;
it also says that in a single thought one knows all phenomena.
Therefore, the one is all, and all is the one.
Therefore, it is said that all things are brought to completion through the efficacy of a single dharma, giving rise to the myriad phenomena.
Thus, a sutra says: "If all things exist, having a mind is delusion;
if all things do not exist, being without a mind pervades the ten directions."
Therefore, the true One is ten thousand differences, and ten thousand differences are the true One.
It is like the ocean surging with a thousand waves: the thousand waves are themselves the ocean.
Thus, all things are one and there is no difference between them.
Now, to speak of "one" is to respond to the notion of "otherness.
Since otherness is not truly other, oneness is likewise not truly one.
That which is neither one nor non-one is the provisional designation for true oneness.
Now, that which is truly one cannot be described by names or words.
Therefore, it is not through a single perception that one perceives the One;
if there were anything perceived, there would be duality.
It cannot be called true oneness,
nor can it be called knowing oneness.
If one knows one, that is called two, and it is no longer called one.
If there is that which is known, then there is ignorance; if there is knowledge and yet no knowing, then there is duality.
Therefore, great wisdom is without knowing, yet there is nothing it does not know;
it is a constant, blazing awareness.
One always knows that there is no knowing; it is a provisional designation for "knowing.
It is not the self, nor what belongs to the self, nor the mind, nor the intellect.
Indeed, where conditioned phenomena exist, there is that which is known.
If unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛtadharma) are like space, having no boundaries or limits,
then there is neither knowing nor not-knowing.
Now, the reason why the Sage speaks of "knowledge" is that there is mind,
there are numbers, there are conditioned activities, and there are dharmas;
therefore, it can be known.
The reason it is said that there is no cognition is that,
being without mind, without number, without conditioned activity,
and without phenomena, it cannot be known.
If one were to use that which possesses knowledge to know that which is without knowledge,
such a thing is impossible.
It is like a person who speaks of emptiness all day long.
However, when people speak of emptiness, it is not a teaching that speaks of emptiness.
If one uses that which knows to know the knowerless,
it is likewise so.
Now, as for why the Sage sometimes says "I know," it is entirely in response to delusion regarding phenomena;
it is intended to break through afflictions and eliminate doubts, for in reality there are no two [truths].
To know is itself non-knowing.
The reason for speaking of non-knowing is that those foolish people do not understand true oneness.
Because they are attached to "self" and "what belongs to self," they falsely imagine a knower and the known;
therefore, it is said that there is no knowledge and no conceptual discrimination.
Upon hearing this, those fools immediately set out to study "non-knowledge."
It is just as a foolish person who cannot discern;
therefore, based on that delusion, the Sage declares that the Tathāgata possesses clear and perfect knowledge and vision.
It is not that they do not know;
rather, as soon as foolish people hear it, they immediately study and come to possess knowledge.
Because they possess this knowledge, there arises the obstruction of knowledge.
This is also called empty knowledge and also called deluded knowledge;
such knowledge further deviates from the Way.
Therefore, the Sūtra says: "Sentient beings associate with evil friends and cultivate evil knowledge and views."
Why is this? Because those non-Buddhists know the future beforehand,
know the past afterward,
and know the body and mind in the present.
Because body and mind are impure, one cannot escape birth and death.
Now, all those who study "non-knowing" discard knowing in order to study non-knowing.
That which is without knowledge is itself knowledge;
yet one does not realize this oneself.
Furthermore, there are those who abandon the state of non-knowing to study the state of knowing.
To know is to have awareness.
Because there is awareness, the mind gives rise to ten thousand concerns and the intellect stirs up a hundred thoughts;
thus, one still does not escape suffering.

He realizes that both views are incapable of corresponding with reality; being empty and harmonious in their essence, they merely accord with principle in a hidden manner, and thus he cannot enter into true reality.
Now, true reality is free from both knowing and not-knowing.
It transcends all limits and measures.
For seeing implies spatial direction,
and hearing implies a specific location.
To awaken is to have a mind;
to know is to have a measure.
One does not realize that the fundamental limit is directionless, placeless, mindless, and immeasurable.
Thus, there is nothing that can be seen, heard, sensed, or known. Therefore,
while the reality is truly one and without duality,
it manifests as different.
Furthermore, there may be someone who, when mindful of the Buddha, the Buddha appears;
when mindful of the Sangha, the Sangha appears.
Yet, that [appearance] is neither the Buddha nor not the Buddha.
Yet they manifest as Buddhas;
even that which is neither the Sangha nor non-Sangha,
they manifest as the Sangha.
Why is this? Because that mind of recollection manifests as a longing, one does not realize that it is a manifestation of one's own mind.
The dependent origination of noble phenomena appears with distinctions solely as external objects.
In reality, there is no difference between the Buddha and the Sangha.
Thus, a sutra says: "They see various Buddha-lands and physical bodies as being manifold;
yet their unimpeded wisdom is not manifold."
For example, it is like a magician who, by the power of illusion,
conjures various forms and images in the midst of space;
because that illusory person is deluded, he thinks that these things existed in the space beforehand.
His mindfulness of the Buddha and the Sangha is likewise thus within the dharma of emptiness.
By the power of the faculty of recollection (*smṛti*), one conjures various forms and appearances, giving rise to deluded perceptions.
Therefore, a sutra says: "The mind is like a stage performer; the intellect (*manas*) is like the master of ceremonies;
the five consciousnesses are its companions, and together they observe the troupe of deluded perceptions."
It is, for example, like a person who, at the side of a great furnace,
fashions a mold of his own— square, round, large, or small— and makes this vow:
"May that molten gold flow into my mold to take the form of an image."
Thus, when molten gold is cast into the form of an image,
its true nature is the fused gold itself;
it is neither the image nor not the image, yet it manifests as an image.
The recollection of the Buddha and the Sangha is likewise so.
That which is called "great wisdom melting gold" is a metaphor for the Tathāgata.
The form of the Dharmakāya is a metaphor for sentient beings;
because they aspire to attain Buddhahood, they practice the recollection of the Buddha (buddhānusmṛti).
Through the convergence of causes and conditions, various bodily forms arise.
However, that Dharmakāya is neither with characteristics nor without characteristics.
What is meant by "neither with characteristics"? It is that, fundamentally, there are no fixed characteristics.
What is meant by "neither non-characteristic"?
It refers to the characteristics of dependent origination.
Thus, the Dharma-body is neither manifest nor non-manifest.
It is free from both existence and non-existence; it is neither existent nor non-existent,
without mind and without volition, and cannot be measured by any means of cognition.
However, those ordinary persons follow their own minds and immediately give rise to the thought that they see a Buddha;
they unilaterally claim that the Buddha exists outside of their mind, not realizing that he exists through the harmonious integration of their own mind.
To claim categorically that there is no Buddha outside of the mind is itself to slander the True Dharma.
Therefore, a sutra states: "The realm of the sages transcends both non-existence and existence; it cannot be measured."
If one clings to existence and non-existence, this constitutes the two extremes and is likewise false. Why?
Because these two views arise delusively and deviate from the true principle.
For example, it is like a person who, within a storehouse of golden vessels,
constantly contemplates the substance of gold and does not perceive its various forms;
although he perceives those various forms, they are all one and the same gold.
Since one is no longer deluded by signs, one immediately becomes free from conceptual discrimination;
one constantly contemplates the golden essence as being without error or falsehood.
The True Person is also like this:
they constantly contemplate the true unity and do not perceive manifold characteristics;
yet even when perceiving manifold characteristics, these are likewise the true unity.
Being far removed from false conceptualization and free from inversion,
one who dwells in the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) is called a noble one (ārya).
Furthermore, suppose there were a person within a treasury of golden vessels.
One constantly perceives various appearances but does not perceive the golden essence;
one discriminates between good and evil,
giving rise to all manner of views.
Yet, having lost sight of the nature of gold,
they engage in disputes;
the foolish person is just like this.
Constantly observing the physical forms of men and women— whether beautiful or ugly— one gives rise to various distinctions;
deluded regarding one's original nature, one clings to mental appearances,
and through grasping and rejecting, loving and hating, one gives rise to all manner of perversions.
Wandering through birth and death, one assumes various bodies;
delusive thoughts proliferate, obscuring the true unity.
Therefore, the gentleman who cherishes the Way and the person of penetrating clarity and realization—
Contemplating the profound, one distances oneself from all categories of phenomena;
this accords with true unity and corresponds to the ultimate principle.
Now, true unity is difficult to express.
Using analogies to explain the ultimate principle of the Way, it cannot be demonstrated through words.
For if one perceives the eye as the eye, one gives rise to the inversion of the eye;
if one perceives the eye as being without an eye, one gives rise to the inversion of no-eye.
Both are false imaginings.
If one clings to the existence of eyes, one is deluded regarding the absence of eyes;
because of this clinging to the existence of eyes, the wondrous vision fails to penetrate.
Therefore, the Sūtra says: "There is no eye and no form, yet there is further delusion regarding the eye.
To treat the eye as being without an eye is to lose one's true eye;
it is like a person born blind who cannot distinguish colors.
Therefore, a sutra says: "For example, a man whose sense organs are destroyed can no longer derive benefit from the five desires. So it is with the śrāvakas;
only the Tathāgata possesses the true divine eye."
Constantly abiding in samādhi, they see all the buddha-fields;
because they do not perceive them through dualistic marks, they are not like ordinary people who have something seen.
Because they are able to see them all, they are not like śrāvakas who have nothing seen.
Those who hold these two views falsely perceive existence and non-existence;
however, within true oneness, the essence is neither existent nor non-existent—
it is only through deluded conceptualization that existence and non-existence are falsely established.
Now, when the Sage says, "I see clearly," or sometimes says,
"I do not see," he speaks of seeing and not seeing solely for the purpose of destroying afflictions.
However, within the single reality of true suchness, there is neither seeing nor non-seeing;
it transcends the boundaries of measure and limit, as well as the stages of ordinary beings and sages.
Therefore, one is able to see with perfect clarity that which is not false or illusory.
Therefore, because it is not a dharma of form, it is not seen by the fleshly eye;
because it is not a dharma of realization, it is not seen by the Dharma-eye.
Only the Buddha-eye, which is pure, neither sees nor does not see.
It is seen with perfect clarity;
it is inconceivable and immeasurable, beyond the reach of ordinary beings.
The two vehicles are like mustard seeds;
Bodhisattvas are like fine gauze.
Thus, one knows that the Buddha-nature is difficult to perceive.
Nevertheless, a sutra states that buddha-nature is universal and applies to both ordinary beings and sages alike;
since it is to be realized within one's own body as the true oneness, what need is there to seek it externally?
Having contemplated this deeply day and night, it was personally realized within my own mind.
Thus, a sutra says: "Contemplate the true mark of the body; contemplate the Buddha in the same way.
Now, contemplating the true mark of the body is precisely the single mark.
The single characteristic is precisely the characteristic of emptiness.
Because it is empty and without characteristics, it is neither defiled nor pure;
it is neither ordinary nor holy, neither existent nor non-existent, and neither deviant nor correct.
The essence-nature is eternally abiding, neither arising nor ceasing; this is precisely the primordial limit (*pūrvakoṭi*).
Why is it that the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body eyes, ears, nose, tongue, and even the body and mind—its various faculties—are mutually interchangeable?
Its essence is truly one,
because it is limitless and without division or measure; thus,
the Dharma-body is empty and pervasive, unimpeded in all things.
Why is it that the various faculties of ordinary beings, such as the eyes and ears, do not interpenetrate and thus lack mutual function?
It is because their faculties are partitioned by the boundaries of deluded conceptualization,
and their spirit and mind are limited.
Because the boundaries of their respective portions are not interpenetrated, they are deluded regarding the single principle of reality and thus fail to function interchangeably.
Therefore, the Sūtra says: "The delusive ignorance of ordinary beings' conceptual consciousness is obstructed and does not interpenetrate."
Through attachment to the faculties and their objects, various distinctions arise.
Therefore, the sage penetrates the true oneness;
they possess no deluded mind that creates boundaries between the faculties and their objects.
Therefore, they are able to function in common without the mental constructs of the mind.
What is meant by "True Unity"? It is because the True is without differentiation.
Because there is no differentiation, the myriad things contain this One within them as they arise.
Thus, those myriad things are also one.
Why? Because they are fundamentally one;
therefore, there is no duality.
For example, when a *dán* tree produces branches from a *dán* tree,
they are ultimately not *chūn* wood. Yet, while that which is truly one possesses various names,
despite these various names, they ultimately share a single meaning.
It is also called the nature of phenomena (dharmatā),
the dharma-body (dharmakāya),
and suchness (tathatā).
The reality-limit,
space, and the Buddha-nature.
Nirvana, the dharma-realm,
and even the ultimate limit.
The Tathāgatagarbha has immeasurable names, all of which are merely different designations for the same reality;
they share the single meaning of "arising together."
The first three chapters are likewise so.
For what reason is this chapter titled "Extensive Illumination"?
It is because the mirror of wisdom is broad and pervasive, and the sun of insight shines perfectly upon all.
It encompasses physical forms, voids, and all spiritual beings;
therefore, it is called "Universal Illumination.
What is meant by the "Chapter on Subtlety and Coarseness"?
That which is called "nature" (xing) encompasses the ultimate truth and reaches the profound source.
The reality-limit (bhūtakoṭi) is empty and void, fundamentally pure and untainted;
therefore, it is called "transcending the subtle" (liwei).
What is meant by the "Chapter on the Original Limit"?
It refers to the wondrous principle of innate truth, whose essence is luminous and not produced through cultivation;
its nature is fundamentally empty and pervasive, encompassing and containing all phenomena.
Therefore, it is called the "Chapter on the Original Limit" (Benji-pin).
For this reason, the preceding three chapters are combined;
a single principle encompasses them all, yielding inexhaustible applications.
Collectively, these are called the "Treasury of Jewels.
Thus, it elucidates the repository of meaning for the myriad phenomena and discusses the fundamental causes and conditions of all things.
The Great Clarity is void and cavernous;
the subtle principles of the Yin Fu are profound.
Those who perfect these find their essence united with the True One.
Those who realize this attain a secret and profound awakening;
thus they clarify the suchness of the Dharma-realm and manifest the essentials of the Great Way.
The Treasure Store Treatise concludes.
